articles.text: Piedmont, by Piedmont, for Piedmont. Subscribe to the Post and we’ll deliver Editor: I want to strongly second what Alli Cota shared in her letter this week. I joined the Calendar Committee towards the end of their process and served on APT’s negotiations team. Both groups focused closely on the parent survey and spent hours examining every possible alternative that would let us start later without moving finals back to mid-January. In the end, we rejected all options that would have started school the first week of August, though that had been our solution for several years. Of course, we also talked with students about their preferences and needs. And as teachers, we have our own understanding of how even small changes to the calendar impact curricula and student success. Teachers’ calendar votes aren’t based on personal preference– teachers aren’t eager to start school in early or mid-August, and find a five-day first week of school exhausting. In fact, the traditional fall semester calendar ending in January was actually easier on secondary teachers: with mid-December finals, we spend much of the holiday “break” feverishly grading. But again and again, we vote for calendars we believe are overall best for the kids. Shortening fall semester doesn’t just impact semester classes–though those are most intensely impacted, with Civics teachers saying they can scarcely cover legally-required state standards in the current semester split, and couldn’t reasonably do so if even more fall classes are cut. Currently, I only teach yearlong courses, but given the critical importance of fall semester grades for college admissions, I feel a deep obligation to ensure my students are truly ready for summative assessments before Winter Break. pages.text: Wednesday, November 26, 2025 3 LETTERS - MAIN Careful school calendar considerations By Allison Cota Editor: As Chair of the Calendar Committee, I’d like to respond to the suggestion that the results of the recent vote didn’t account for the interests of families. In truth, the Committee closely examined the Parent Survey results twice. And, since every teacher and CSEA member on the Committee has sent their kids through Piedmont schools, we had the lens not only of educators, but of fellow parents in the district. Building possible calendars is simultaneously straightforward and complex – a shift of just one day creates a domino effect that impacts the rest. The parameters are strict: proposed calendars must include 180 student and 185 staff days, prevent the loss of Average Daily Attendance (ADA), abide by Federal holidays and have semesters of approximately equal length. Additionally, all stakeholder groups clearly indicated that Fall semester should end before Winter Break, including 71.5% of parents on the survey. The Committee also considered calendars of many nearby districts before drafting and weighing the merits and challenges of 9+ different options of our own. We were required to propose one model mirroring our current calendar, plus at least three others. Negotiating teams then evaluated our recommendations; ultimately district leadership asked to replace two with their own. One mirrored 2025-2026, two started one day later by moving a day from Fall to Spring, and the fourth started a full week later, but at the cost of pushing the end of first semester to mid-January. Teachers then voted based on what they believed would best serve the interests of our students. The “cur rent” calendar received 80 of 158 votes, as compared to 35, 24, and 19 respectively for the others. While the winning calendar received “only” just over 50%, it received more than twice as many as the next runner up, and won by a landslide 34 to 6 at the high schools. According to the feedback we’ve received, the main reason for that choice was avoiding further unbalancing the semesters. Two years ago, when asked to move the start of school later than the first week of August, teachers agreed to move from an 88/92 to an 87/93 semester split. For those not in the classroom, moving one day still farther, to an 86/94 split, might seem minor. However, the combined loss of two 90-minute periods in the Fall, nearly a week of instruction, (and an 8-day difference from Spring), while having to cover the same content and skills with less time, forces teachers to make difficult decisions: do we cut out essential topics/standards? push more assignments into homework? remove engaging activities that reinforce key concepts? eliminate opportunities for in-class feedback? While returning to school on a Monday is not ideal, many felt the cost of further truncating Fall semester would have been considerably worse for our classes. Additionally, there’s a strong argument to support student days-off throughout the school year. These days provide muchneeded opportunities to catch up with coursework, allow time with family/friends, and help protect student social-emotional health at a time when they may need it substantially more than at the close of ten weeks of summer. And interestingly, it’s not true that “feedback strongly favored a mid-week start”; 53.1% of parents indicated that was “not at all important”; only 13.9% responded it was “very important”. While I understand that some are frustrated that APT did not vote the way they preferred, it is my hope that my comments will help to clarify how we got here. Both groups focused closely on the parent survey and spent hours examining every possible alternative that would let us start later without moving finals back to mid-January. In the end, we rejected all options that would have started school the first week of August, though that had been our solution for several years. Of course, we also talked with students about their preferences and needs. And as teachers, we have our own understanding of how even small changes to the calendar impact curricula and student success. Teachers’ calendar votes aren’t based on personal preference– teachers aren’t eager to start school in early or mid-August, and find a five-day first week of school exhausting. articles.text: A warm welcome with a sweet treat, Lisa Chan Carnazzo, Broker Associate with The Grubb Company, hosted multiple neighborhood celebrations to introduce her clients to their new community. One gathering took place on Harvard Road, complete with a soft-serve ice cream truck and a visit from Piedmont Police Chief Frederick Shavies. Longtime neighbors, newer neighbors, and friends stopped by to say hello and share an ice cream cone in honor of the city’s newest homeowners. Chief Shavies praised the event’s community-building spirit, saying, “This is an absolutely incredible event. You have soft serve out here, you have children from the elementary school, middle school, and high school, and you get to know new families. It’s a great opportunity, and I’m happy my team and I were actually invited.” Also in attendance was Officer Tyler Petit, who echoed the department’s support of neighborhood engagement. “I love coming to these because it’s a great opportunity for the new owners to understand the level of service they’ll receive in Piedmont. We respond to every call and provide the best level of service possible,” said Petit. These events are part of a growing tradition Carnazzo has created, using her “Local with Lisa” platform and real estate expertise to not only secure homes for her clients but to instantly connect them with the community they are joining. As neighbors mingled along the sidewalk, children enjoyed swirls of vanilla and chocolate ice cream, and new homeowners were greeted with warm handshakes and friendly conversation. The gatherings showcased what Piedmont is known for: a close-knit community that welcomes with intention and a little extra sweetness. Photo courtesy of Lisa Chan Carnazzo Party on Harvard Rd. articles.text: The City of Piedmont and the Piedmont Beautification Foundation (PBF) are partnering to install new swings in the Tot Lot at the Main Park. This project comes closely on the heels of their collaboration to do a spectacular renovation of the Linda Beach Tot Lot, to which PBF contributed $100,000. Last year, the swings at the Main Park were removed for safety reasons, and Piedmont grandmothers, parents, and nannies have been lamenting their absence ever since. Swings bring a special kind of joy to a tot lot, and PBF has agreed to raise funds to return this joy to the Main Park. Residents should watch for their LIGHTS UP PIEDMONT brochures, which will arrive in mailboxes soon. In addition to announcing that this year’s Lights Up Ceremony will take place at 6 p.m. on Wednesday, December 3, the brochure highlights the Main Park Swings Project as this fall’s primary campaign focus. The redesigned swing area will feature: • State-of-the-art materials for durability and safety • Safety matting to replace the existing sand • An expanded play area providing a secure perimeter for enthusiastic swing lovers This year’s PBF brochure offers plenty of alternative opportunities for the community to support its ongoing work. Funds are still needed for the Sydney Dearing Memorial, and the “reforest Piedmont” project has become a long-term effort of great significance. PBF’s two endowment funds, the Sports Facilities Maintenance Endowment and its general Endowment, are both worthy of support. Donors can return their gifts in the envelope accompanying the brochure or by visiting the PBF website: piedmontbeautificationfoundation.org. The brochure’s most important function is to invite all residents to this year’s Lights Up Piedmont ceremony at 6 p.m. on Wednesday, December 3. articles.text: During the November 12 Piedmont School Board meeting, action was taken to approve a $0 premium cost healthcare option for teachers. The district has agreed to pay the full premium for teachers who select the single-party High Deductible Health Plan (HDHP). The district estimates a cost of $55,673 per year for providing this option to the Association of Piedmont Teachers (APT), but that number depends on how many employees select that specific plan. After the approval, now all district employees have a zero-premium, high-deductible plan option; CSEA school employees and school administrators approved the option last year. “I’m thrilled APT has opted to take advantage of this benefit that our other bargaining groups had already opted into,” said School Board President Lindsay Thomasson. The zero premium options is a high deductible health plan, which is great for exceedingly healthy people that never go to the doctor. However, if one actually needs health care, they can expect to pay a lot of money, out of pocket, very quickly. “Because signing up for HDHP is a fairly risky thing to do, very few of our members chose the HDHP plans for 2025. I believe only 11 members out of about 185 chose the 1-party HDHP Kaiser plan last year,” said APT president Elise Marks. She explained that APT did not select the option last year on principle, in 2025 Kaiser offered the single-party HDHP option for only a $23 premium per month. Marks stated that of more importance is that “more and more

articles.text: From bedtime questions to Sunday pancakes, the patterns that hold us together My daughters were twelve when they casually mentioned that Thursday nights were their favorite. Not because anything extraordinary happened . . . we simply made quesadillas together, the same way we had since they were six. They’d grate the cheese while I diced peppers, and we’d talk about nothing in particular. “It’s just ours,” as if that explained everything. And of course, it did. In the blur of school runs, work deadlines, and weekend sports schedules, family life can sometimes feel less like a story and more like a logistics operation. We connect, but it’s often about what’s next: “Did you finish your homework?” “Who’s driving to soccer?” We crave connection, but the “how” gets lost. What if the “how” isn’t a grand, week-long vacation, but something we already have, hidden in plain sight? What if it’s in the way we say good morning, the specific board game we pull out on a rainy day, or the one question we ask at the dinner table? You’re Already a Ritual-Maker Most households already have rituals . . . they just don’t notice them. The way you greet each other in the morning, the bedtime rhythm, the micro-conversations in the car, the joke you repeat so often your kids pretend to hate it . . . those are rituals. They’re the background music of childhood. And once you see them, you can shape them. This is good news because rituals don’t need to be elaborate or time-consuming. They don’t require themed tablescapes, color-coded calendars, or anything Pinterest would applaud. They just need to be intentional, recurring, and meaningful to the people involved. How do you spot them? Ask yourself: • What do your kids complain about when it doesn’t happen? • What small thing would feel wrong to skip, even when you’re exhausted? • What phrase, gesture, or moment happens the same way every time—a particular goodbye, a weekend breakfast routine, the way you always end the day? • What would a visitor to your home notice that you do “your way”? Maybe it’s the knock-knock joke your seven-year-old insists you tell every morning on the drive to school. Perhaps it’s how your teenager still lets you play “your song” when you pick her up from practice. It might be the way everyone gravitates to the kitchen on Sunday mornings, knowing pancakes are coming, or how Friday night means pizza and a family movie. Your Ritual Shopping List: From Micro-Moments to Milestones Some are tiny (10 seconds). Some take a bit more effort. Some happen daily, while others yearly. And yes, holidays already give us rituals. The goal isn’t to do them all; it’s to find a handful that feel like your family. Check out the table of rituals like going shopping or visiting a store for inspiration. The rituals that stick are the ones that feel easy, that fit your family’s particular rhythm and humor and needs. Don’t force it. But don’t underestimate the quiet power of showing up, in the same small way, again and again. The Invitation You don’t need to adopt a dozen new rituals this month. Start with one. Or start by simply naming and cherishing the ones you already have. Tell your kids: “I love our Thursday quesadillas.” They’re surprisingly easy to start. Pick something your family genuinely enjoys, tie it to a time or trigger, repeat it, and watch it grow. In the end, rituals are how we become the kind of family we like being—one pancake, car-ride playlist, or bedtime question at a time. And years from now, when your child casually mentions that Thursday nights were their favorite, you’ll know exactly why. The district estimates a cost of $55,673 per year for providing this option to the Association of Piedmont Teachers (APT), but that number depends on how many employees select that specific plan. After the approval, now all district employees have a zero-premium, high-deductible plan option; CSEA school employees and school administrators approved the option last year. “I’m thrilled APT has opted to take advantage of this benefit that our other bargaining groups had already opted into,” said School Board President Lindsay Thomasson. The zero premium options is a high deductible health plan, which is great for exceedingly healthy people that never go to the doctor. However, if one actually needs health care, they can expect to pay a lot of money, out of pocket, very quickly. “Because signing up for HDHP is a fairly risky thing to do, very few of our members chose the HDHP plans for 2025. I believe only 11 members out of about 185 chose the 1-party HDHP Kaiser plan last year,” said APT president Elise Marks. She explained that APT did not select the option last year on principle, in 2025 Kaiser offered the single-party HDHP option for only a $23 premium per month. Marks stated that of more importance is that “more and more local districts are actually paying the full premium for real, low-deductible Kaiser coverage, even for a full family. Albany is doing that,” she said. “APT felt there was no point in refusing the district’s offer to cover the Kaiser 1-party HDHP plan, which would have been going up to a $181 premium because of the huge jump in Kaiser premiums for 2026,” Marks added. “Because our Kaiser plans are skyrocketing for 2026 (increasing on average about $500 per month compared to 2025 rates), I’m guessing more educators will switch to HDHP for 2026 just to be able to afford health care at all,” said Marks. Between January 1 and June 30, 2026 the district will offer the $0 premium employee-only HDHP option. Not because anything extraordinary happened . . . we simply made quesadillas together, the same way we had since they were six. They’d grate the cheese while I diced peppers, and we’d talk about nothing in particular. “It’s just ours,” as if that explained everything. And of course, it did. In the blur of school runs, work deadlines, and weekend sports schedules, family life can sometimes feel less like a story and more like a logistics operation. We connect, but it’s often about what’s next: “Did you finish your homework?” “Who’s driving to soccer?” We crave connection, but the “how” gets lost. What if the “how” isn’t a grand, week-long vacation, but something we already have, hidden in plain sight? What if it’s in the way we say good morning, the specific board game we pull out on a rainy day, or the one question we ask at the dinner table? You’re Already a Ritual-Maker Most households already have rituals . . . they just don’t notice them. The way you greet each other in the morning, the bedtime rhythm, the micro-conversations in the car, the joke you repeat so often your kids pretend to hate it . . . those are rituals. They’re the background music of childhood. And once you see them, you can shape them. This is good news because rituals don’t need to be elaborate or time-consuming. They don’t require themed tablescapes, color-coded calendars, or anything Pinterest would applaud. They just need to be intentional, recurring, and meaningful to the people involved. How do you spot them? Ask yourself: • What do your kids complain about when it doesn’t happen? • What small thing would feel wrong to skip, even when you’re exhausted? • What phrase, gesture, or moment happens the same way every time—a particular goodbye, a weekend breakfast routine, the way you always end the day? • What would a visitor to your home notice that you do “your way”? Maybe it’s the knock-knock joke your seven-year-old insists you tell every morning on the drive to school. Perhaps it’s how your teenager still lets you play “your song” when you pick her up from practice. It might be the way everyone gravitates to the kitchen on Sunday mornings, knowing pancakes are coming, or how Friday night means pizza and a family movie. Your Ritual Shopping List: From Micro-Moments to Milestones Some are tiny (10 seconds). Some take a bit more effort. Some happen daily, while others yearly. And yes, holidays already give us rituals. The goal isn’t to do them all; it’s to find a handful that feel like your family. Check out the table of rituals like going shopping or visiting a store for inspiration. The rituals that stick are the ones that feel easy, that fit your family’s particular rhythm and humor and needs. Don’t force it. But don’t underestimate the quiet power of showing up, in the same small way, again and again. The Invitation You don’t need to adopt a dozen new rituals this month. Start with one. Or start by simply naming and cherishing the ones you already have. Tell your kids: “I love our Thursday quesadillas.” They’re surprisingly easy to start. Pick something your family genuinely enjoys, tie it to a time or trigger, repeat it, and watch it grow. In the end, rituals are how we become the kind of family we like being—one pancake, car-ride playlist, or bedtime question at a time. And years from now, when your child casually mentions that Thursday nights were their favorite, you’ll know exactly why. The team’s equipment currently is kept in a storage facility in Richmond. They are currently paying $125 a month in rent to store their gear. Recently, the facility was broken into, and a loaner bike was stolen from their trailer. Reining has a growing concerned about the safety of their gear. “It strikes a blow. Anytime anything is stolen it kind of hits your sense of security,” said Reining. “Our loaner bikes are primarily used to recruit more girls to the team. The team prides itself on its female representation, so the loss of a bike can harm recruitment. The mountain biking team includes 23 athletes from Piedmont High School and 25 members from the middle school. For every race, the team brings a trailer stocked with the equipment and supplies needed to compete. Not only is the trailer a functional part of the team, but an important part of their publicity efforts. The team utilizes the trailer to raise awareness and support recruiting efforts through participating in local community events. Most notably they were visible as an entry in Piedmont’s Fourth of July Parade. Reining believes moving the storage location to Piedmont would make things easier for their volunteer coaching staff. “It can take around 45 minutes to an hour to take the trailer out of storage and back,” Reining added. “It’d be really great to find a parking space somewhere inside the city of Piedmont. We’d love to have this trailer in town, closer to home.” According to the mountain biking team’s petition, “We are asking the broader city, school district and various facilities management organizations within the City of Piedmont to provide one parking space for the trailer. The team is happy to pay market-rate rent for the parking space.” The petition launched on October 20 has more than 150 signatures supporting the team’s goal to find parking in Piedmont. This event is a book talk and an open conversation about the search for meaning, meaningful encounters, and the drive to keep exploring the world. The beauty of nature as a catalyst for inner transformation and the quiet power of gratitude are other themes recurring in the book. Federica is currently visiting from Italy—more precisely from an area between Tuscany and Rome called Tuscia (pronounced too-shah), where the novel is set. The story’s main character has recently settled in Tuscia, and she discovers the territory guided by a local friend and—lacking a better word—her “angel.” As if the landscape weren’t stunning enough, their friendship-turned-romance adds emotional depth, as she recounts the journey in retrospect, inviting us into her memories. The trip began at Heart’s Desire Beach near the small town of Inverness, where 19 scouts and 15 parents mounted their kayaks to start a journey of nature and beauty through the waters of the bay. After two hours of kayaking and sightseeing, the troop finally landed on the campsite. It was a small, quiet beach with a view of the golden hills, surrounded by trees and the sounds of birds. The next day, we embarked on our journey back to Hearts Desire Beach where we encountered choppy waves and harsh winds, which managed to steer many of our kayaks off course. Even on the way back with the harsh climate on our backs, we still managed to enjoy the beauty of Tomales Bay State Park. articles.text: Piedmont High’s No. 2 seeded football team made school history on Friday, November 21. It is the second team in school history to qualify for the North Coast Section Championship game after beating No. 3 Willits 28-10 in the NCS semifinals at Witter Field. They are now set to square off in the Division 7 title game against No. 1 Middletown this Friday, November 28 at Justin Siena High School in Napa. The 1976 NCS title-winning Hall of Fame squad and this year’s team are the only Championship game appearances in Piedmont High’s 100-plus year history. “I was just three years old. I’ve said before, not a lot of people thought we’d be here. The guys stuck with it through my ranting and raving. They never wanted to quit and they never lay down,” said Piedmont head coach Jordan Seiden. It’s a miraculous moment for the football program, considering it lost eight seniors from last year’s team and fell in the Dov. 8 NCS semifinals on Ferndale’s swampy playing surface. This is the first time Piedmont has reached the semifinals in two consecutive years. It has appeared in the semifinals in 1976, 1981, 2014, 2016, 2024, and now 2025. “We’re in the history books. It’s amazing; we couldn’t get it done last year. We had the talent, but had to play in tough field conditions,:” said running back and linebacker Xavier Henderson. “I don’t even know what to say; so many words come to mind. We’re making history and hopefully we can get that win to make history next Friday,” added quarterback Jimmy Lagios. Piedmont had to lean on its defense to keep Willits out of the end zone. The HighlandStaff Photos Piedmont football players stand proudly after beating Willits 28-10 in the D7 NCS Semifinals. Their championship game this Friday marks the school’s first since 1976. ers didn’t score the game’s first touchdown until 3:43 remained in the first quarter, and the Wolverines stayed just one possession back of the lead through three quarters of the game. But once PHS figured out Willits’ rushing attack, Ferndale struggled to finish drives. “To start the game, they were chipping off small plays, and their big drive came from some big plays. We knew if we did our jobs, we’d be fine. Once our offense started going, it forced them to pass. Our coverage is really good, and their throws were all screens, so we just had to focus on tackling,” middle linebacker Colby Hong said. Henderson, the team’s star running back, made his presence felt on defense as a linebacker. On offense he led the team with three rushing touchdowns. “I give all credit to my offensive line, as always. I couldn’t do anything without them,” Henderson said. “Defensively, I haven’t played in a few weeks because of a concussion. I had to step up and play for the team. There’s a lot to correct still, but that’s football; we live to fight another day.” Game Recap After trading possessions to start the game, Piedmont struck first with 3:34 remaining in the first quarter when Rehan Mumtaz punched across a two-yard carry. The previous play, Henderson broke a tackle to take a carry 26 yards to the two. Willits answered on its next possession, scoring on a 12-play series at the 10:56 mark of the second quarter, which capped off with a 31-yard touchdown carry on a 4th-and-4 situation. PHS wound up punting on its next possession, but thwarted Willits on 4th-and-1 at the Highlanders’ 16, where linebacker George Saunders burst through the line to stop a fullback carry. PHS then scored on a nineplay series with 32 seconds left in the half. The drive featured a 23 yard carry my Mumtaz, a 47-yard reception by Diego Hurwitz down to the three, and capped by a touchdown by Henderson. In the third quarter, more back-and-forth possessions led to a 34-yard field goal by Willits with 2:20 left, cutting Piedmont’s lead to 14-10. But PHS’ offense came alive with two touchdowns in the fourth quarter. The Highlanders scored on its next possession, taking it 64 yards on eight plays, finishing with a two-yard score by Henderson with 10:39 left. During the series, PHS had chunk plays of 16 and 15 yards by Henderson, and 18 and 12-yard receptions by Cash Panico. Piedmont then forced another turnover on downs at Willits’ 45 with 6:25 left, leading to a 12-play touchdown series with 1:44 remaining in the game. Jack Meyjes had a 12 yard reception, Henderson had a 14-yard run where he stiff-armed a defender to the floor, while Henderson scored on a six-yard carry. Final game stats were not provided. pages.text: 12 Wednesday, November 26, 2025 Sports Piedmont punches ticket to first NCS Championship game since 1976 By Jonathan Comeaux Piedmont High’s No. 2 seeded football team made school history on Friday, November 21. It is the second team in school history to qualify for the North Coast Section Championship game after beating No. 3 Willits 28-10 in the NCS semifinals at Witter Field. They are now set to square off in the Division 7 title game against No. 1 Middletown this Friday, November 28 at Justin Siena High School in Napa. The 1976 NCS title-winning Hall of Fame squad and this year’s team are the only Championship game appearances in Piedmont High’s 100-plus year history. “I was just three years old. I’ve said before, not a lot of people thought we’d be here. The guys stuck with it through my ranting and raving. They never wanted to quit and they never lay down,” said Piedmont head coach Jordan Seiden. It’s a miraculous moment for the football program, considering it lost eight seniors from last year’s team and fell in the Dov. 8 NCS semifinals on Ferndale’s swampy playing surface. This is the first time Piedmont has reached the semifinals in two consecutive years. It has appeared in the semifinals in 1976, 1981, 2014, 2016, 2024, and now 2025. “We’re in the history books. It’s amazing; we couldn’t get it done last year. We had the talent, but had to play in tough field conditions,:” said running back and linebacker Xavier Henderson. “I don’t even know what to say; so many words come to mind. We’re making history and hopefully we can get that win to make history next Friday,” added quarterback Jimmy Lagios. Piedmont had to lean on its defense to keep Willits out of the end zone. The HighlandStaff Photos Piedmont football players stand proudly after beating Willits 28-10 in the D7 NCS Semifinals. Their championship game this Friday marks the school’s first since 1976. ers didn’t score the game’s first touchdown until 3:43 remained in the first quarter, and the Wolverines stayed just one possession back of the lead through three quarters of the game. But once PHS figured out Willits’ rushing attack, Ferndale struggled to finish drives. “To start the game, they were chipping off small plays, and their big drive came from some big plays. We knew if we did our jobs, we’d be fine. Once our offense started going, it forced them to pass. Our coverage is really good, and their throws were all screens, so we just had to focus on tackling,” middle linebacker Colby Hong said. Henderson, the team’s star running back, made his presence felt on defense as a linebacker. On offense he led the team with three rushing touchdowns. “I give all credit to my offensive line, as always. I couldn’t do anything without them,” Henderson said. “Defensively, I haven’t played in a few weeks because of a concussion. I had to step up and play for the team. There’s a lot to correct still, but that’s football; we live to fight another day.” Game Recap After trading possessions to start the game, Piedmont struck first with 3:34 remaining in the first quarter when Rehan Mumtaz punched across a two-yard carry. The previous play, Henderson broke a tackle to take a carry 26 yards to the two. Willits answered on its next possession, scoring on a 12-play series at the 10:56 mark of the second quarter, which capped off with a 31-yard touchdown carry on a 4th-and-4 situation. PHS wound up punting on its next possession, but thwarted Willits on 4th-and-1 at the Highlanders’ 16, where linebacker George Saunders burst through the line to stop a fullback carry. The drive featured a 23 yard carry my Mumtaz, a 47-yard reception by Diego Hurwitz down to the three, and capped by a touchdown by Henderson. In the third quarter, more back-and-forth possessions led to a 34-yard field goal by Willits with 2:20 left, cutting Piedmont’s lead to 14-10. But PHS’ offense came alive with two touchdowns in the fourth quarter. The Highlanders scored on its next possession, taking it 64 yards on eight plays, finishing with a two-yard score by Henderson with 10:39 left. During the series, PHS had chunk plays of 16 and 15 yards by Henderson, and 18 and 12-yard receptions by Cash Panico. Piedmont then forced another turnover on downs at Willits’ 45 with 6:25 left, leading to a 12-play touchdown series with 1:44 remaining in the game. Jack Meyjes had a 12 yard reception, Henderson had a 14-yard run where he stiff-armed a defender to the floor, while Henderson scored on a six-yard carry. Final game stats were not provided. articles.text: They did it. Chad Ironside’s U19B Piedmont soccer team won the California Cup regional rec tournament in Fremont on Saturday and Sunday, November 22-23 without conceding a goal. They played four matches, winning by scores of 4-0, 4-0, 4-0, and 1-0 to take the trophy, beating teams from Sunnyvale, Los Gatos and San Ramon. “This is the best possible way to wrap up 9+ years coaching some of these boys before they go off to college. I couldn’t be more proud. Thanks to Aaron Murdock, Neil McKee and everyone else that has helped us coach and manage these boys through the years,” head coach Chad Ironside said. This completes a fall season in which they compiled a perfect 14-0-0 record, scored 61 goals and conceded only eight. “Anyone who has played team sports knows that 14-0-0 is special. Of course we still get no more than a nonchalant shrug from the boys. I suspect, however, that when they look back they will remember this with a smile,” assistant coach Neil McKee said. This ragtag bunch of misfits, waifs and strays has been playing together for nine years. In recent seasons they found success locally even when playing older teams. But over the summer those older rivals finally graduated and left, leaving Piedmont in the unfamiliar position of being the older and stronger squad. “I’m particularly proud of the players that have been with us for so many years and have devoted themselves to improving and having fun. It is also a testament to Piedmont’s ongoing commitment to recreational soccer. Relatively affluent communities are so often railroaded into believing that expensive competitive or traveling teams are the only way their children can learn and enjoy sports. I think we’ve proven that model to be false. We have produced successful varsity players as well as players who simply love to come out and have fun playing,” assistant coach Aaron Murdoch said. They trained twice a week at Beach Field, bringing energy and effort every night. Several players represented Piedmont High School at Varsity and Junior Varsity level, which accelerated their development. But rec soccer is not just about winning on smooth surfaces with sharp-eyed referees and a row of eager subs on the bench. It requires adapting to “ploughed field” surfaces, unpredictable refereeing, confrontational opponents and days when only 9 or 10 players make it to kickoff. That makes it all the more remarkable that the boys were able to pull off this 14-0-0 season, and lift the regional trophy. Piedmont’s U-19 team had a perfect 14-0-0 season on their way to winning the California Cup, including head coach Chad Ironside (left), Miles Kim, Leyton Poole, Rimoni Puni, Elias Reed-Miguel, Sean McKee, Theo Lois-Gleeson, Bodie Ironside, Ry Laby, Declan Murphy, assistant coach Aaron Murdock, Lucas Ironside, Leighton McClure, Declan O’Connel, Matti Hesse (Clippers), Liam Armstrong (Clippers), Neil McKee, Peter Murdoch (not pictured), and Maxim Gorodnichenko (not pictured).

articles.text: Staff Photos Ben Russell and the defending D5 CIF NorCal champion boys’ soccer team returns to the pitch on December 3 at Skyline in Oakland. Piedmont High’s boys soccer team opens its regular season on Wednesday, December 3, with a visit to Skyline High in Oakland. The Highlanders return to the pitch after winning last year’s Division 5 CIF NorCal title and finishing as runners-up in the Division 4 North Coast Section tournament. The Highlanders will have big shoes to fill with nine seniors from the Class of 2025 having graduated. Up top, Piedmont will have to replace lead striker Gianluca Bini, who scored a hat trick in the team’s 4-1 NorCal title win over Williams. Several younger players are stepping into key roles. Sophomore Ben Gerber and freshman Evan Yamanaka are already making an impact, while sophomore Robert Piniella returns as a starter from last season. “It’s going to be quite different to go from a 6’5” senior to younger players. It’s a slightly younger team, but we’re not just setting the standard for this season, but for years to come. That’s why it’s important to get these young guys in and get them prepared,” coach Ben Russell said. The attack could get a late-season boost from junior Derin Sabuncuoglu once he returns from his club’s MLS Next schedule. Sabuncuoglu scored in Piedmont’s 2-0 win over Colusa in last year’s NorCal semifinals and is currently on trial with USL Championship side Sacramento Republic, which is the second division of U.S. professional soccer. “He’s on trial at Sacramento Republic, but we will try to get him involved at the right time of the season again. He’ll practice when available and join when there’s a gap in his MLS Next season,” Russell said. The departure of Harper Mand opens a spot in the midfield, but senior Henry DeVan returns and has been named a team captain. Roman Ahearn looks set to take over the central attacking midfield role. Ahearn proved to be a vital playmaker and set-piece specialist last season. “Roman Ahearn is gonna be a crucial part of it, as well as Henry DeVan, who is going to be a captain. Henry plays as a six, and Roman as a ten,” Russell said. Piedmont’s backline will also feature new faces following the graduations of Max Goldfarb and Jacques Saldanha. Freshman Cole Venner is stepping in as the starting right back, while sophomore Maxwell Rodriguez is a player to watch at center back. “We have a very young back line. Cole Venner is a freshman and did a really great job in a scrimmage. Maxwell Rodriguez is a brother of Jacob Rodriguez, who graduated. He’ll be at the heart of our back line,” Russell said. Of course we still get no more than a nonchalant shrug from the boys. I suspect, however, that when they look back they will remember this with a smile,” assistant coach Neil McKee said. This ragtag bunch of misfits, waifs and strays has been playing together for nine years. In recent seasons they found success locally even when playing older teams. But over the summer those older rivals finally graduated and left, leaving Piedmont in the unfamiliar position of being the older and stronger squad. “I’m particularly proud of the players that have been with us for so many years and have devoted themselves to improving and having fun. It is also a testament to Piedmont’s ongoing commitment to recreational soccer. Relatively affluent communities are so often railroaded into believing that expensive competitive or traveling teams are the only way their children can learn and enjoy sports. I think we’ve proven that model to be false. We have produced successful varsity players as well as players who simply love to come out and have fun playing,” assistant coach Aaron Murdoch said. They trained twice a week at Beach Field, bringing energy and effort every night. Several players represented Piedmont High School at Varsity and Junior Varsity level, which accelerated their development. But rec soccer is not just about winning on smooth surfaces with sharp-eyed referees and a row of eager subs on the bench. It requires adapting to “ploughed field” surfaces, unpredictable refereeing, confrontational opponents and days when only 9 or 10 players make it to kickoff. Team captains included Nuala Price and Chloe Hong, who helped create and nurture a positive environment where the girls showcased their dedication to both academics and tennis. articles.text: The City of Piedmont and the Piedmont Beautification Foundation (PBF) will host the annual tree lighting ceremony at Community Hall on December 3. PBF will keep last year’s earlier start time of 6 p.m. to make the event easier for younger guests. The celebration will feature the illumination of an 80-foot redwood tree and a menorah, along with activities for both children and adults. Santa will be available in Community Hall starting at 5:30 p.m. for photos. Piedmont Girl Scouts and the Recreation Department will host an activity table where children can create a light-themed art project and play games. Inside Community Hall, children can write letters to Santa using the provided supplies, including colored pencils, paper and envelopes. Volunteer “elves” will be on hand to help, and a special mailbox with express delivery to the North Pole will be available for drop-off. Food and drinks have been donated by local groups eager to contribute to the holiday celebration. Piedmont Boy Scouts will serve hot cider donated by Piedmont Grocery and hot cocoa supplied by the Heafey-Baum Group. Recreation Department staff will offer latkes, gifted by the Chabad Jewish Center. Music will be performed by the Piedmont High School Troubadours, the student-run a cappella group. After brief remarks from Piedmont mayor Betsy Smegal Andersen, a Make-AWish Foundation recipient will flip the switch to light the 80-foot redwood, the menorah and the surrounding greenery throughout the park. Attendees will receive a fiber-optic light wand so everyone can take part in lighting up Piedmont together. This community tradition began in 1969 as Piedmont’s tree lighting ceremony. Now in its fourth year under the name Lights Up Piedmont, the event has grown to include symbols of winter light celebrations from around the world. The 80-foot Redwood tree lit up Staff photo

articles.text: The Asian Art Museum’s newest exhibition, Rave into the Future: Art in Motion, is on view now through January 26, 2026. The exhibition spotlights women and queer artists from the West Asia diaspora currently based in the United States and Europe and is inspired by West Asian rave and underground music culture. Oakland-based Arab Persian American artist Sahar Khoury contributes a multimedia sculpture equipped with a functioning DJ deck that will be activated by local Asian and Asian diaspora DJs. Los Angeles–based Yemeni American artist Yasmine Nasser Diaz’s installation For Your Eyes Only recreates an intimate bedroom where projections of dancers, archival clips, and protest materials form a layered portrait of generational expression and activism. Disguise as Dancefloor, a nearly 100-square-foot copper dancefloor by London-based Lebanese American artist Joe Namy, is designed to record the footsteps of visitors while symbolizing the healing properties associated with the material across cultures. Other featured pieces bring humor, futurism, and fantastical narrative into the mix, including Meriem Bennani’s Party on the CAPS, Sophia al Maria and Fatima al Qadiri’s bass-driven Spiral, and Farah Al Qasimi’s horror-comedy Um Al Naar. The exhibition culminates in a glitter-filled “after-party” animated by robotic vacuum cleaners in Puff Out by the Brussels-based duo :mentalKLINIK. Curated by Naz Cuguoğlu, Assistant Curator of Contemporary Art, the exhibition has already earned significant recognition. Cuguoğlu received a curatorial research fellowship from The Andy Warhol Foundation for the Visual Arts last year, and the museum was recently awarded an additional foundation grant to bring the project to fruition. “I wanted to create a space for narratives that build solidarity through joy, pleasure, and laughter,” Cuguoğlu said, noting the need to counter dominant Western portrayals of West Asia rooted in Orientalism and suffering. “This exhibition asks what we can learn from the autonomy, healing, and bliss that unfold on the dancefloor,” Cuguoğlu said. Museum Director and CEO Soyoung Lee added that the show offers a timely opportunity to broaden public understanding of West Asia while celebrating the universal joy of collective dance.
articles.title: Rave into the Future on view now at Asian Art Museum

articles.text: Eight performances presented in SF, Berkeley and Sonoma State University The beloved, annual holiday concert series returns next month. The San Francisco Gay Men’s Chorus ushers in the holiday season this December with its annual Holiday Spectacular concert series, presenting eight performances across the Bay Area and continuing a decades-long tradition of music, community and festive flair. Led by Artistic Director Jacob Stensberg, the 2025 program blends classic seasonal arrangements with the chorus’s signature camp, humor and theatrical energy. Event organizers said audiences can expect heartfelt choral harmonies, showstopping production numbers and a celebratory atmosphere designed to bring “joy, laughter and glitter” to the holidays. Chorus leaders said this year’s program is designed to offer a sense of unity and celebration for audiences of all ages, including families and “chosen families” throughout the region. The long-running holiday event remains one of the Bay Area’s most anticipated seasonal traditions, drawing thousands each year for a blend of musical artistry, community spirit and holiday exuberance. The series opens in San Francisco at the Golden Gate Theatre, located at One Taylor St., with performances scheduled for December 12 at 7:30 p.m. and December 13 at 1 p.m. and 7:30 p.m. Tickets start at $35. The following weekend, the chorus travels to the East Bay for two shows at Zellerbach Hall in Berkeley organized by Cal Performances. Those concerts take place December 20 at 2 p.m. and 8 p.m., with tickets ranging from $43 to $98. The Holiday Spectacular continues on December 21 at 5 p.m. at the Green Music Center’s Weill Hall at Sonoma State University in Rohnert Park. Tickets for that performance range from $31 to $118. The series concludes Christmas Eve with “Home for the Holidays – Special Christmas Eve Edition” at Davies Symphony Hall in San Francisco. Performances are scheduled for December 24 at 4 p.m. and 7 p.m., with tickets starting at $35. Tickets for all performances are available online at https:// www.sfgmc.org/welcome/.
articles.title: San Francisco Gay Men’s Chorus launches “Holiday Spectacular” performances on Dec. 12

articles.text: American Conser vator y Theater (A.C.T.) presents the acclaimed holiday tribute musical Judy Garland: We Need a Little Christmas, showing at Strand Theatre in San Francisco December 6 and 7. London native Debbie Wileman marks her San Francisco debut with A.C.T.’s production of We Need a Little Christmas fresh off the release of her new holiday album A Christmas Garland. Wileman impersonates a range of classic female singers of Hollywood’s Golden Age, including Shirley Bassey, Marilyn Monroe, Julie Andrews and Billie Holiday, but her uncanny recreation of Judy Garland’s famous vocals garnered her a massive online following and worldwide recognition. She teams up with producer Scott Stander to perform a touring concert of Garland’s famous holiday hits including “Have Yourself a Merry Little Christmas,” which Garland introduced in the 1944 movie Meet Me in St. Louis, and “The Christmas Song,” which she performed with Mel Tormé on The Judy Garland Show. A.C.T.’s Strand Theater is located at 1127 Market Street in San Francisco. Judy Garland: We Need a Little Christmas is showing on Saturday, December 6 at 7:30 p.m. and Sunday, December 7 at 2 p.m. Tickets are on-sale now at www.act-sf.org. articles.text: Dancers in Rex Wheeler’s “Snow Day!” Smuin Contemporary Ballet’s annual holiday production “The Christmas Ballet” is touring the Bay Area with performances in Carmel, Mountain View and San Francisco next month. “The Christmas Ballet” is a popular ensemble of 31 short dance pieces, ranging from classical to swing to step dance and Broadway and featuring holiday classics like “Santa Baby,” “Joy to the World” and “Silver Bells.” Showtimes for the 2025 production tour vary. “The Christmas Ballet” will be presented at Sunset Center in Carmel December 5 and 6; at Mountain View Center for the Performing Arts in Mountain View December 11 through 14; and at Blue Shield of California Theater at Yerba Buena Center for the Arts in San Francisco December 18 through 28. Visit https://www.smuinballet. org/ for more information and to purchase tickets. Most of the choreography is by the dance company’s founder, Michael Smuin, who died in 2007. Along with a return to Smuin’s original pieces, the company will also reveal new works this year by Smuin Ballet’s Dance Director Julia Adam, Artistic Director Amy Seiwert, and San Francisco Ballet Soloist Myles Thatcher. Smuin’s beloved “Santa Baby,” featuring the “world’s longest feather boa” rounds out the two-act performance. After the concert, I spoke with pianist Amy Zanrosso and asked her who made the arrangement. She responded that everything came together, and that the musicians did not need to make any adjustments. It was fun watching the individual players. In one particular piece, bass player Ken Miller dazzled the audience with his harmonics. Carnival of the Animals served as an appetizer for what came next. This was the variation movement from Schubert’s “Trout” quintet. Perhaps they will play the entire quintet next time. The all-too-brief concert came to an end with Sacha Jacobsen’s arrangement of Gershwin’s Rhapsody in Blue. It is quite amazing how adaptable this composition is. Exactly one week ago there was a solo piano version of Rhapsody. That version was fabulous and so was the yesterday’s version for piano and string quintet. Bravo to all of the performers and to arranger Sasha Jacobsen. Sending all of you warmest regards for a beautiful Thanksgiving…
articles.title: Smuin Ballet presents “The Christmas Ballet” in San Francisco Dec.18 - 28

articles.text: ‘Twas the week before Thanksgiving Ogden Nash was preparing his animal parade in Piedmont’s Center for the Arts last week as six musicians served up a memorable concert on Sunday afternoon: violinists Beni Shinohara and Karen Shinozaki, viola Paul Ehrlich, cello Victoria Ehrlich, bass Ken Miller, piano Amy Zanrosso and narrator Danny Slomoff. Entitled “Carnival, Trout, and Blue,” the concert was a success from beginning to end. St.-Saens’ composition, Carnival of the Animals, opened the program. Curiously, the composer had some misgivings about his masterpiece and forbade its publication. If he had witnessed Sunday’s performance, he would have been overjoyed. Narrator Danny Slomoff delivered the delightfully clever poems by Ogden Nash with appropriate relish. So did the six musicians. It was obvious that they had fun at every turn, including subtle sarcasm alongside understated virtuosity. Those of us in the audience who were watching noticed smiles on the faces of the musicians. Ogden Nash’s poems always produce laughter from the audience. It was obvious that they understood everything perfectly. Piedmont’s Center for the arts concert on Sunday featured violinists Beni Shinohara and Karen Shinozaki, pianist Amy Zanrosso, violist Paul Ehrlich, cellist Victoria Ehrlich, bassist Ken Miller, and narrator Danny Slomoff. A scene from How to Train Your Dragon: The Hidden World How to Train Your Dragon: The Hidden World is the final installment of what has been a very successful franchise, the first released in 2010. This last chapter may lack the punch and freshness of the earlier films, but it is beautifully animated, with glorious scenes of dragons in flight circling the island refuge of Berk. This medieval village, home to a cohort of Vikings now led by the aspirational chief Hiccup (Jay Baruchel) and supported by his girlfriend Astrid (America Ferrera), is filled with memorable characters both young and old. And of course Hiccup’s best friend Toothless, a rare alpha dragon, is alive and well, and the two still ride the skies as one. Again, the computer graphics are breathtaking. This is no longer your grandfather’s painstaking, Disneyesque animation. There is, naturally, a villain, a malevolent dragon hunter named Grimmel (F. Murray Abraham) who speaks with a curious accent. His mission is to kill Toothless and control the dragons who live peacefully in Berk. Fortunately, he is a bit of a klutz, good at plotting, less so at carrying out his schemes. Unexpectedly, there are two budding love stories in this film. One, telegraphed in the previous installments, is between Hiccup and Astrid, who are now talking about marriage. The other involves Toothless and a kindred female dragon who, unlike his obsidian scales, is white as snow. It is hard not to wonder how these romantic threads will play for an audience still well below tween age. Still, the dialogue is charming and lightly contemporized, though Hiccup never quite ventures into “Dude!” territory. The final act, which takes Hiccup and Astrid to the Hidden World, is remarkable, a feast of color. Having found this sanctuary at the edge of the world, Hiccup understands that Toothless and his new companion finally have a true home. Separation is inevitable. Or perhaps not. In the end, there is more than enough here for young viewers to fully say goodbye to a delightful crew of dragon riders and their dragons. How to Train Your Dragon: The Hidden World. The route up Linda Avenue would also take them to a few streets they had not visited yet this year. The walkers headed down Magnolia Avenue and paused to admire the new Community Pool. It is beautiful, though they knew the opening had been delayed because of equipment issues. Walker and Post cartoonist Phil Witte refers to it as “the pool of the future,” and the group agreed that the name fits. The $400,000 project was funded 75% by the City’s Facilities Capital Fund, with the remaining 25% coming from a $100,000 donation from the Piedmont Beautification Foundation (PBF). The PBF has a long history of supporting play areas in every major park in town, including Dracena, Main Park and Hampton Field. The redesigned tot lot reflects months of outreach and surveys with parents, caregivers and young users who offered feedback on their favorite features. The new play area includes updated equipment, a bright and welcoming theme, swings, low climbing structures sized for ages two to five, an enclosed layout and classic elements like slides and steps. Interactive panels and balance features encourage imagination and movement. The new rubber matting surface is ADA compliant and provides additional safety. A new water fountain is also in place. The group could not go inside, but the sidewalk offered enough space for a group photo to mark their reconnaissance mission. With the morning still young, the walkers continued up Linda past Beach School and on to the 900 block of Kingston Avenue. The street, repaved this year, looked terrific. articles.text: The culinary cognoscenti have proclaimed flavors of the Eastern Mediterranean are all the rage, and for good reason. These tasty spice and herb combinations are familiar, but with an exotic twist. The good news for us is there are numerous options to procure them for your home’s kitchen. I find it is easier to try out a few prepared spice blends when venturing into new flavor territory to learn what suits my taste buds. Inevitably after a few uses I start “doctoring” the blend – adding here, subtracting there, until I start making my own concoctions. Such is the case for ras el hanout, a spice blend originating in North Africa. It translates from Arabic to “top of the shop,” implying the best spices available go into the mix. While there are many versions (some with dozens of ingredients), most include cumin, ginger, cinnamon, cardamom, coriander, turmeric, cayenne, allspice, cloves, salt and pepper – spices found in most well-stocked pantries. You might notice these are also very warming spices – perfect for cold winter days. Starting with a prepared blend, this soup comes together very quickly, under 30 minutes. This recipe is perfect for adapting according to your tastes and what you have available. After all, it’s soup – so there’s a wide range to navigate! pages.text: 26 26 Wednesday, November 26, 2025 WINE CORNER The Wine Corner Napa Valley Wine Tasting Featuring Lewis Cellars and Elyse Winery By Pierre DuMont For anyone who has tried to go wine tasting in Napa Valley recently you know that it is not exactly an easy task. Not that there is any scarcity of wineries; Napa now hosts over 500 wineries. It’s just that prices for tastings have increased so much in recent years that the cost becomes prohibitive. Also, some of the better wineries are booked out weeks in advance. So, I was delighted on a recent trip to Napa to have the opportunity to taste at two totally different wineries. On the luxurious end of the spectrum, I visited Lewis Cellars who just opened an opulent new tasting room on Silverado Trail 5 days before my visit. On the other end of the scale representing an old school winery was Elyse Winery who offered a casual down-home tasting experience that was simple and perfect. Here is a run-down on some of the current releases of each winery. Lewis Cellars Lewis Cellars was started in 1992 by former Indy racer Randy Lewis and his wife Debbie and later joined by their son Dennis. Over the years the Oak Knoll area winery gained notoriety for producing outstanding Chardonnay, Cabernet Sauvignon, and Syrah. The little winery won outstanding accolades from the wine press including a “Wine of the Year” from Wine Spectator magazine. In 2021 the Resnick family bought Lewis Cellars along with the Robert Sinskey Winery on Silverado Trail. They decided to turn the Sinskey property into a luxurious world class wine tasting showroom. Randy Lewis and Dennis Bell remain involved with leadership under the new structure. When I approached the tasting room last month three attendants in black suits, white shirts and bolo ties greeted us with a glass of Sauvignon Blanc and nonstop patter about the new tasting room. It was obvious no expense had been spared. The furniture was luxurious, the fabrics ornate, the walls adorned by beautiful custom designed art and the wall to ceiling glass windows offered a stunning view of Napa Valley. In addition to the wines, they served delicious culinary tidbits created by their on-site chef and designed to pair specifically with the wines. It was one of the most luxurious tastings I have experienced anywhere. • 2023 Lewis Sauvignon Blanc Matured in oak and stainless steel the Lewis Sauvignon Blanc features subtle toast and lees notes and a hint of hazelnut to go along with guava, pear and fig. It’s on the ripe side flavor wise while being medium bodied with a softly, creamy feel on the palate and a long silky finish. Excellent aperitif. • 2023 Lewis Chardonnay Russian River Valley Two Chardonnays to us at the tasting. One was a big buttery old style Napa Valley Chard which was just a bit over the top. Then there was this wine from the Russian River Valley which was leaner with much less oak on the nose. It has lemon citrus flavors that were refreshing in the mouth with great acid and fine balance. Both wines were well made but we preferred this style. • 2022 Lewis Cabernet Sauvignon This wine is blended with some Merlot and Cabernet Franc and aged in 75% new French oak. The wine begins with aromas of cherries and currants with some herbal notes. In the mouth, the wine is medium to full-bodied, The view of Napa Valley from Lewis Cellars. The Elyse tasting room is a throwback to simpler days in Napa Valley. silky textured and elegant, with hints of toasty oak and red berries lingering on the finish. Not particularly tannic, it should be approachable within a few years and drink well for at least 15. • 2022 Lewis Big Blend This is a mélange of Syrah, Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Cabernet Franc and Petite Sirah. It unwinds in the glass with notes of cassis, plums, violets and black pepper. On the palate, the wine is bold, velvety and full-bodied, with lots of crunchy fruit and good juicy acidity, as well as excellent concentration and length. This saw 65% new oak, but it is not obtrusive and provides great structure and a hint of vanilla. • 2023 Lewis Full Circle This is Cabernet Sauvignon, Syrah and Petite Sirah. It used to be considered an anathema to combine a Bordeaux grape like Cabernet and a Rhone grape like Syrah. This wine proves how silly that rule was. It combines the best of both worlds with an ebullient nose that bounds out of the glass followed by blackberry, plum and black cherry flavors on the palate. It is big bodied with a round mouthfeel, extremely complex, it has just the right amount on tannins on the satisfying finish. Elyse Winery Our next tasting was at the opposite end of the Napa Valley luxury continuum. Elyse Winery is about as far as you can get from the opulence of Lewis. The tasting room is housed in a humble wood building and our tasting was outdoors under a trellis on a wooden picnic table. It was very old school and like the Napa I visited 20 years ago. Nestled in the heart of Napa Valley on Hoffman Lane just south of Yountville, Elyse Winery is a beloved, small-producThe knowledgeable Garett Lyon directs the Elyse tasting room. tion estate known for crafting deeply expressive, vineyard-designate red wines. Founded in the mid-1980s by Ray and Nancy Coursen, Elyse started in 1987 with just 286 cases of Zinfandel sourced from the historic Morisoli Vineyard. Over the decades, the winery has built a reputation for fruit-forward authenticity, focusing especially on Zinfandel, Cabernet Sauvignon, and Petite Sirah. In 1997, the Coursens purchased their own hilltop property with a rustic barn-turned-tasting room, anchored by just 1.5 acres of estate vines and set among quiet Napa vineyards. Elyse is celebrated for its commitment to expressing “sense of place”: each wine reflects the unique soils, climate, and farming of its source vineyards. In 2018, the winery passed to new owners Josh Peeples and Cheryl Foil but retained its traditional ethos under talented winemaker Russell Bevan. The new ownership under the name HQ also added additional brands Addax and Institution. Additionally, a pair of climbers in another party nearly suffered asphyxia by using a camp stove in their tent without sufficient ventilation. After two weather days, Baringer and the group ventured to Camp Four at 17,255 feet, despite forecasts of 60+ mph winds. In the words of singer David Lee Roth, “I guarantee, you will find no reasonable men on top of big mountains.” They woke up the next morning and found no new snow from the night and relatively light winds. The guides told them if they couldn’t summit in eight hours, they were turning around regardless. Baringer headed up the “autobahn” section, an ironically named extremely steep and slow slope. The weather turned out to be great and they summited in 6 ½ hours, giving them extra time at the summit. Having conquered another behemoth of a mountain, Baringer checked off number five on his list of the world’s highest peaks on each of the seven continents. pages.text: 32 32 Wednesday, November 26, 2025 Cross-Country Continued from page 13 Boys Results Piedmont’s boys’ cross-country team came away with a ninthplace finish in a field of 18 teams at the North Coast Section championship meet. Sophomore Dresden Schulte-Sasse led the squad in 29th of 130 runners with a time of 17:09.58, junior Alex Schleuning was 33rd in 17:14.47, sophomore Photos by Jenni Tsoi Best Viviane Oesterer, a sophomore, was one step behind Best in 25th. Aaron Bennett finished 37th in 17:28.65, freshman Dylan Wallway was right behind in 38th in 17:30.27, while Ian Chung rounded things out in 67th in 18:08.51. Bennett emerged as a lead runner this season, but had to persevere on Saturday while dealing with an injury he suffered during in practice during the week “The younger runners led the way for our boys’ team. Dresden had the best race of the day, Dylan also raced well in the slippery conditions. Aaron Bennett sustained an injury earlier in the week and still managed to be our third runner despite running through a great deal of pain,” Zirkelbach said. NEXT UP Piedmont heads to the CIF State Championship at Woodward Park in Fresno on Saturday, November 29. Rather, we focus on family, friends, health, love, memories and the joy of life itself. We reflect with gratefulness on these wonderful gifts as we gather to share a special meal. The words of a hymn written in 1846 express it well: For the beauty of the earth, For the glory of the skies, For the love which from our birth Over and around us lies, Lord of all, to Thee we raise This our hymn of grateful praise. The community of friends and neighbors that is Piedmont Community Church wishes you and yours a happy and heartwarming Thanksgiving. You are invited to experience all that Piedmont Church has to offer throughout the holiday season of Advent and into the New Year. Cole Hitchcock is another fantastic goalkeeper. We have great depth at that position, so I’m really excited about them,” Russell said. Last season, the Highlanders finished 13-4-9 in Russell’s first year as head coach, steadily building into his system as the season progressed. By year’s end the squad was thriving, beating opponents in transition and on counterattacks. With many players to replace, Russell is focused on reestablishing his structure with a younger group. “We’re notably very young after having nine seniors last year, where all nine of them were starters. That inexperience is something we’ll have to overcome with the physicality and the speed of play. It’s them understanding how to up that intensity,” Russell said. Piedmont opens the season with two road matches in as many days, starting at Skyline on December 3 and continuing at Newark Memorial on December 5. Henry DeVan returns to the midfield as a team captain. Ben Russell hopes to get Derin Sabuncuoglu back from his club schedule in time for the postseason. He could make a big difference late in the season. Where in the World Are We?
